ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
As shown in the figure, the insulating rough horizontal track $AB$ (with a coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu=0.5$) is smoothly connected to a semicircular insulating smooth track $BC$ in the vertical plane, where $BC$ is the vertical diameter. The radius of the semicircular track is $R=0.4\,\mathrm{m}$. In the space where the track is located, there is a uniform electric field directed horizontally to the right, with the electric field lines parallel to the plane of the track. The electric field strength is $E=1\,\mathrm{N/C}$. A charged object (which can be treated as a point particle) with charge $q=+1\,\mathrm{C}$ and mass $m=0.1\,\mathrm{kg}$ is released from rest at point $P$ on the horizontal track. The charged object just manages to pass through the highest point $C$ of the semicircular track and then lands at point $D$ on the horizontal track (not shown in the figure). The acceleration due to gravity is taken as $g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

1. What is the speed of a charged body when it moves to point $C$ on a semicircular track?
2. What is the distance $x_{PB}$ from point $P$ to point $B$?
3. At which point does the charged object have the maximum kinetic energy as it moves from point $B$ to point $C$? And what is the maximum kinetic energy (rounded to two significant figures)?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
$2\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$
$2\mathrm{m}$
When the motion reaches the point where the line connecting the charged body and the center of the circle forms a $45^{\circ}$ angle with the vertical direction, the kinetic energy is at its maximum, with the maximum kinetic energy being $1.2\mathrm{J}$.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: At the bottom of the figure is a rough horizontal track AB, with A at the left end, and the charged small block moves rightward from point P on the horizontal track to point B; point B is tangentially connected to the smooth semicircular track in the vertical plane on the right side. The semicircular track is on the right side of the vertical diameter BC, B is the lowest point, C is the highest point, O is the center of the circle, and the radius R is marked in the figure. Multiple horizontal electric field lines all point to the right and are marked as E. Reasoning: At point C, "just passes through the highest point"; according to the specified method, take the critical condition N=0. At point C the radial direction is downward, and the electric field force is horizontally to the right, not providing a radial component, so mg = m v_C^2 / R; therefore v_C = sqrt(gR) = sqrt(10 × 0.4) = 2 m/s. Thus K_C = (1/2) m v_C^2 = 0.5 × 0.1 × 4 = 0.2 J. From B to C, the track is smooth; B and C are on the same vertical line, and the horizontal displacement is 0, so the total work done by the electric field force is 0. The gravitational potential energy increases by mg(2R), so K_B = K_C + mg(2R) = 0.2 + 0.1 × 10 × 0.8 = 1.0 J. From P to B, on the horizontal track, the electric field force does positive work qE x_PB to the right, and the friction force of magnitude μmg does negative work μmg x_PB to the left. By the kinetic energy theorem: (qE - μmg)x_PB = K_B. Substituting qE = 1 N, μmg = 0.5 × 0.1 × 10 = 0.5 N, gives 0.5 x_PB = 1.0, so x_PB = 2 m. Find the maximum kinetic energy from B to C. Let θ be the angle from the vertically downward OB to the radius line connecting to the particle; then relative to O there are x = R sinθ, y = -R cosθ. From B to that point, the electric field does work qER sinθ, and gravity does work -mgR(1 - cosθ). Therefore K(θ) = K_B + qER sinθ - mgR(1 - cosθ). Set the derivative to zero: dK/dθ = qER cosθ - mgR sinθ = 0, namely qE cosθ = mg sinθ. Because qE = 1 N and mg = 1 N, tanθ = 1, θ = 45°. Substituting gives K_max = 1.0 + 1 × 0.4 × sin45° - 1 × 0.4 × (1 - cos45°) = 1.1656 J, approximately 1.2 J to two significant figures.

claims.label: reasoning
claims.source: Let the derivative be zero

claims.claim: Let dK/dθ = 0 to obtain qE cosθ = mg sinθ; substituting qE = mg = 1 N gives θ = 45°.
claims.label: reasoning
claims.source: Set the derivative to zero: dK/dθ = qER cosθ - mgR sinθ = 0, that is, qE cosθ = mg sinθ. Because qE = 1 N and mg = 1 N, tanθ = 1, θ = 45°

claims.claim: Substituting θ = 45° gives K_max = 1.1656 J, approximately 1.2 J to two significant figures.
claims.label: reasoning
claims.source: Substitute into K_max = 1.0 + 1 × 0.4 × sin45° - 1 × 0.4 × (1 - cos45°) = 1.1656 J, approximately 1.2 J to two significant figures
